sample_student_quotes: When I write 'class Dog', that creates a Dog instance in memory ready to use.
I thought defining the class allocated the object fields immediately.
So a class alone creates the object without calling new.
A class and an object are essentially the same thing in Java/C++.
Both hold the methods and allocate memory when declared.
CLASS_IS_AN_OBJECT.remediation_suggestion:
Pedagogical Intervention:
  Writing `class Dog` defines what a Dog looks like. No Dog exists in memory until you write `new Dog()`. How many Dogs exist after `class Dog` alone? Zero.
Key Takeaway: Writing `class Dog` defines what a Dog looks like. No Dog exists in memory until you write `new Dog()`. How many Dogs exist after `class Dog` alone? Zero.

PRIVATE_MEMBERS_INHERITED.remediation_suggestion:
Pedagogical Intervention:
  If private members were accessible in subclasses, the private keyword would provide no encapsulation. Any internal refactoring of the parent would silently break the child's direct field access. The fields exist in the child object's memory, but the child's code cannot name them.
Key Takeaway: If private members were accessible in subclasses, the private keyword would provide no encapsulation. Any internal refactoring of the parent would silently break the child's direct field access. The fields exist in the child object's memory, but the child's code cannot name them.
